extracted.intended_audience: general readers and stand-up comedians interested in comedy, race, and performing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical principles for stand-up comedians (particularly Muslim or minority performers) about writing personal material, handling racist hecklers, and portraying race on screen/stage. Focuses on authenticity, avoiding stereotypes, and stagecraft for dealing with abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize identity-based material
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as it's in a way that's very personal to myself... as long as I'm really talking about my experience I can trust that it'll be unique and it won't be like hack or anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your own lived experience when addressing identity (e.g., being Muslim) onstage. Framing material as personal reduces the risk of relying on tired stereotypes and makes the material feel unique. Anti-pattern: discussing identity only as a set of stereotypes or generic complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid playing to stereotypes / don't be 'hack'
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as I'm not like trying to play to stereotypes... I can trust that it'll be unique and it won't be like hack or anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't write jokes that simply reproduce common, lazy stereotypes about a group. If material feels like the 'same pool' many others are dipping into, find a more specific or personal angle. Scoring note: material that relies on stereotype is likely to read as lazy and unoriginal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relatable 'gateway' references to introduce sensitive topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Star Trek jokes are the gateway to Muslim jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with broadly relatable, non-contentious references (pop-culture, geek culture) to build rapport and then transition into identity-related or sensitive material. This eases the audience into tougher subjects. Example: using Star Trek as an entry point before discussing ethnicity or religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict racist characters or behavior to shine a light, but clarify perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to be able to show people being awful and racist and understand that's not the perspective of the show... sometimes depicting people make the mistake of hearing what a character says and think that that's what the movie or TV show is saying when that's not true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing racism onstage or on-screen, ensure the larger narrative or performer perspective makes clear the critique—don't let depiction be interpreted as endorsement. In scripted work, maintain authorial/contextual cues that the viewpoint shown is being critiqued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare canned comebacks for racist hecklers
rubrics_metrics.description: I decided like I would have like a comeback line that I would just like recite back... If someone said something racist to me I would say these three lines back and it would kill cause the audience just wanted you to do something to shut this person down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a few practiced lines ready so you don't have to rely on split-second wit when confronted. A rehearsed, well-phrased comeback can satisfy the audience and defuse the situation. Anti-pattern: freezing or responding angrily without a plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor to defang and assert (rather than escalate)
rubrics_metrics.description: That's right I am a terrorist. I just do stand up comedy on the side to keep a low profile... the stand up comedy camp is actually right next to the terrorist camp. There's very talented people on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn the heckler's insult into a joke that exposes its absurdity; this both defuses the power of the slur and rallies the audience. This technique flips hostility into comedy and reasserts control. Caution: ensure the joke doesn't inadvertently normalize the hate speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn stagecraft by watching others handle hecklers
rubrics_metrics.description: Todd went up on stage after me and really ripped on that person and I was like oh my God that's fantastic. That's what I should have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe veteran performers' responses and adopt strategies that fit your persona; emulating successful shutdowns can inform your own prepared responses. Scoring note: performers who can draw lessons from peers tend to handle disruptions more smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep material current; heckler references age with events
rubrics_metrics.description: So it used to be you know Taliban and now it's Isis. So they keep abreast of... They're hip to the times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the specifics of racist heckles and cultural references change over time. Update examples and responses so they land with contemporary audiences. Anti-pattern: relying on dated references that fail to register with or alienate the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition gradually from observational to personal comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: I had been doing it for five or six years and I was like there's a big part of me that once I started talking about Star Trek and other stuff I liked... then I decided like you know I can talk about being from Pakistan and again talk about my ethnicity and my identity as long as it's in a way that's very personal to myself...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many comedians evolve from broad observational material toward more personal storytelling. Use a gradual shift—leveraging audience rapport built on neutral topics—to introduce deeper personal or identity-focused work.
